title: Two Olympiads, two new leaders: Poland and Czech Republic surge ahead in Samarkand
summary: Day 5 of the 3rd FIDE Chess Olympiad for People with Disabilities marked a special moment in Samarkand. While the competition entered its decisive phase, the Opening Ceremony of the 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad also took place today, meaning that the two Olympiads are now officially running alongside each other in the same host city. Cuba entered the day as the sole leader, but Round 5 dramatically reshaped the standings. Victories for Poland and the Czech Republic left the two teams sharing first place with 9 match points and set up a direct clash between them in Round 6. The ceremonial first move of Round 5 was made by Victor Bologan, FIDE Executive Director, before another important day of competition got underway. Cuba brought to halt as two teams move to the top The headline encounter of the round saw sole leader Cuba face top seed Poland in an extremely close match. Marcin Molenda drew Carlos Larduet Despaigne, Aleksander Czerwonski split the point with Hector Luis Fuentes De Feria, while the game between Julia Salamon and Idalis Batista Rivera produced the same result. The decisive point came on Board 2, where Pawel Piekielny defeated Pedro Morales Romero, sealing a 2½–1½ victory for Poland and handing Cuba its first match defeat of the tournament. The Czech Republic took full advantage of the opportunity against Israel. Three games ended in draws, but Anna Ryvova’s victory over Aleksandra Aleksandrova on Board 4 secured another 2½–1½ result propelling the Czech team into a shared lead. Elsewhere in the leading group, the Philippines defeated Croatia 2½–1½, while IBCA overcame Germany by the same score. The USA beat Argentina 3–1, while Uzbekistan 1 prevailed over Serbia 2½–1½. India scored a narrow 2½–1½ victory over IPCA; Ukraine defeated Belarus 3½–½, while Kazakhstan recorded the same score against Bangladesh. After five rounds, Poland and the Czech Republic lead with 9 match points, closely followed by the Philippines, Cuba and IBCA on 8. USA, Uzbekistan 1 and India are next with 7 points each. Always there to help Behind the games, however, is a large group of people whose work can easily go unnoticed. From assisting arbiters and helping participants to guiding teams around the venue, volunteers are always present and ready to step in wherever they are needed. With the 46th Chess Olympiad now beginning alongside the Olympiad for People with Disabilities, many of them will be supporting both events. Among them is Shahrizoda, one of the Uzbek volunteers working at the Olympiad for People with Disabilities. “We are here, as volunteers of Uzbekistan, to help our players,” she said. “The atmosphere is beautiful and really exciting, and it is motivating us, the volunteers, to be patient and dedicated.” For her, the desire to help others also reflects the hospitality of the host country. “Helping other people is one of the kindest things for Uzbek people as well.” Shahrizoda will continue volunteering during the main Olympiad. She also has her own connection to chess, having played the game for around eight years. “I can’t say I’m a pro, but I can play,” she said with a smile. “Right now, I tried again and I remembered how to play chess.” “Something out of this world” With the Opening Ceremony of the 46th Chess Olympiad taking place on the same day, the presence of the world’s leading players has already created memorable encounters for participants. For Jesus Camilo Osorio of Panama, the experience has made his third Olympiad for People with Disabilities particularly special. “Every time is a dream come true for me to play the Olympiad for people with disabilities,” he said. “And this year it has been more special because we have been able to play at the same time with the Open Olympiad and the female Olympiad.” Osorio, 42, has already managed to meet one of his childhood chess heroes. “First I managed to catch Ivanchuk at the entrance. He was my hero when I was very young, because his chess was so creative.” Then came an encounter with reigning World Champion Gukesh D. “I saw through the door that Gukesh, the World Champion, was coming. And I was like, ‘I have to take a picture with this guy.’” After Osorio took his photo, many others quickly followed. “He was like Michael Jackson. Everybody wanted to take a picture with him,” he joked. But for Osorio, the Olympiad is ultimately about much more than meeting famous players. “Every Olympiad is getting better. It’s very good that we have more teams because we are able to meet more people and make connections in different countries. And after the Olympiad, we keep sharing our knowledge and playing online chess and making new friends.” Chess without barriers Nurnahar Tonima of Bangladesh, the only female player on her team, offered another perspective on what participation in Samarkand means. Tonima has a visual impairment and competes using a Braille chessboard. She began playing chess in 2017 under the guidance of her coach Ijaz Hossain, who also has a visual disability. “It is a very prestigious event for me and my country also,” she said, emphasizing the importance of Bangladesh having a team of players with disabilities competing internationally. Tonima demonstrated how she distinguishes the squares and pieces through touch. “This is a black square and this is a white square. I touch, and I also know where my pieces are and how I play.” Once the position is established on the board, the essence of the game remains exactly the same: calculation, ideas and decision-making. “Chess is very intellectual. It’s not a barrier.” From champion to arbiter The Olympiad also brings together officials whose personal stories are closely connected to the players they are helping. Wilfredo Paulino of the Dominican Republic is working as an arbiter at the event. Having previously attended Olympiads in Azerbaijan in 2016 and Hungary in 2024, he had the opportunity to work at the main Olympiad in Samarkand but chose the Olympiad for People with Disabilities

title: Barcelona 1992 was special; Samarkand was something else: A night unlike any other
summary: Written by Michael A. Rahal, FIDE Press Officer By now, I have attended my fair share of opening and closing ceremonies: Grand Prix events, several World Cups and Olympiads, and even the opening and closing ceremonies of the Barcelona 1992 Olympic Games. But none of them comes remotely close to what the chess community witnessed this evening in Samarkand, Uzbekistan. The Boqiy Shahar Amphitheater, located on the banks of the Silk Road channel, provided a spectacular setting for the opening ceremony of the 46th Chess Olympiad, with more than 2,000 spectators in attendance. Part of Samarkand’s Eternal City complex, the open-air venue was transformed for the occasion into a stage for an evening that brought together chess, music and the rich cultural heritage of Uzbekistan. And what a show it was! For nearly two hours, the audience was treated to a spectacular succession of performances, featuring military units, choreographed dance, opera, traditional costumes and the distribution of sweets in beautifully decorated baskets. More than 100 musicians and over 200 dancers and singers took part in the production, creating an extraordinary show, illustrating the richness and diversity of Uzbek culture. The official part of the evening featured two speeches. First, the Prime Minister of the Republic of Uzbekistan, Abdulla Aripov, conveyed greetings from the President of Uzbekistan. He was followed by a heartfelt five-minute address from Viswanathan Anand, FIDE Interim President and a five-time World Chess Champion. Halfway through the ceremony, the National Anthem of the Republic of Uzbekistan and the FIDE Anthem were performed by the Honoured Choir of Uzbekistan and the State Choir Chapel, adding a solemn and ceremonial moment to the evening. One of the most anticipated highlights of the evening was the traditional drawing of colours ceremony, determining which teams would have the White and Black pieces on the first board in tomorrow’s opening round. The honour of conducting the draw fell to Zhu Chen, the ninth Women’s World Chess Champion, and Rustam Kasimdzhanov, Uzbek chess legend and former FIDE World Chess Champion. The two guests selected pieces of both colours from traditional boxes, with White going to the highest-ranked team in the Women’s section and Black to the top seed in the Open section. The audience was particularly impressed by the spectacular 3D visual mapping and drone light show, which filled the night sky with images of chess pieces and a dazzling array of illuminations. And, to top it all off, a lively pop song and dance brought hundreds of players onto the stage, joining together in a mass celebration as fireworks lit up the sky above them. It was a fitting and unforgettable way to bring the evening to a close. Don’t miss the full show on the FIDE Youtube channel https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oMrfXZbs7oU Photos: Rafal Oleksiewicz and Michal Walusza

title: Opening press conference of the 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad
summary: The high-profile panel, moderated by Charlize van Zyl, featured Viswanathan Anand, FIDE Interim President, Alisher Sadullaev, 1st Vice President of the Uzbekistan Chess Federation, Gulrukhbegim Tokhirjonova, from team Uzbekistan (women’s section) and Nodirbek Abdusattorov, representing team Uzbekistan (open section). Charlize van Zyl set the scene by introducing the guests and drawing attention to the Olympiad numbers: nearly 400 teams participating in the main event, with 208 in the open section and 191 in the women’s section, while the Chess Olympiad for People with Disabilities has also drawn its biggest field. Five-time World Champion, and since July, FIDE Interim President, Viswanathan Anand, was the first guest to speak, announcing some sad news: the passing of Georgios Makropoulos, FIDE Vice President and Honorary President of the Greek Chess Federation. On a brighter note, he went on to explain why the Olympiad is such a treat: “The Olympiad is a record-breaking tournament, with a huge number of teams participating. It’s a place where chess players of all levels compete in the same tournament, a celebration of chess, and that’s what makes every Olympiad special.” Regarding the numerous complaints about accommodation and other organisational issues that had been raised on social media, Anand acknowledged that there had been some problems: “I would like to acknowledge that there have been certain problems that have cropped up, such as the accommodation for participants, accreditation, visas – some teams are having trouble. I just wanted to mention that we are working very hard together with the local organising committee to address these problems. They have already resolved a lot of issues, and I hope that we can resolve the remaining ones as quickly as possible.” Subsequently, Mr. Alisher Sadullaev took the floor. The 1st Vice President of the Uzbekistan Chess Federation, one of the people who has spent the last two years turning this city into a chess venue, welcomed everyone to the event. “This Olympiad is naturally a spotlight for the whole Uzbek chess history and legacy for the world. Uzbekistan has prepared a great number of programs for the whole event. It is one of the hardest challenges because we are organizing three events at the same time: the FIDE Chess Olympiad for People with Disabilities, the FIDE Congress, and the Olympiad itself, for which we have been preparing for four years already.”  The third panelist was Gulrukhbegim Tokhirjonova. Two years ago, she played board one for the United States, helping them secure a bronze medal in Budapest. This week, however, she makes her first Olympiad appearance under the Uzbek colours since 2018. “I was invited back by the Uzbekistan Federation and government, and I was really happy and pleased. I left for some personal reasons but I love my country: my teammates are amazing, and I am happy to play for my team.” Before opening the floor to the rest of the media, Charlize introduced the fourth and final member of the panel. Representing the host nation in the open section, the 2021 World Rapid Champion, winner of Wijk aan Zee this year, and Uzbekistan’s board one when they took gold in Chennai: Nodirbek Abdusattorov. Asked how it felt to be competing at home in front of the local crowd, with the added pressure and responsibility, Abdusattorov said: “It’s a great honour to represent our country at the Olympiad. Samarkand has already hosted several big FIDE tournaments and has a lot of organising experience. Most of the players are familiar with the place and the environment. Compared to the Chennai and Budapest Olympiads, our team has improved a lot in this period: today we have two top ten players, and our third board is over 2700, and I think that we arrive in very good form here.” The full press conference can be viewed on the FIDE YouTube channel. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WahRJ7drJ7Q&t=32s Written by Michael Rahal, FIDE Press Officer Photos: Michal Walusza
